title: Jefferson Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Jefferson wells have a 345 ft median depth, 5.0 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $28,400-$46,500.
h1: Jefferson, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Jefferson means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow aquifer. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 345 feet, with the middle half between 250 and 460 feet. The median reported pump yield is 5.0 gallons per minute.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and most wells are identified with unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. The records are useful for setting expectations, but a nearby well is not a guarantee for your lot. In Jefferson, the driller’s site assessment, access, geology, and the spacing and construction of neighboring wells all matter.

sections.heading: Jefferson wells usually reach fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Depth is the first number to carry into a drilling discussion. Jefferson-area wells have a 345-foot median depth, while the middle half runs from 250 to 460 feet. That range is wide enough that a bid based only on the closest well can be misleading.

About 54% of reported wells are between 300 and 600 feet, and 9% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,950 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; smaller groups identify Fractured Crystalline or Fractured Granite. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures, so depth can change sharply over a short distance. Ask for nearby well logs, not just a countywide average.

sections.heading: A 5.0 gpm median is workable, but not a guarantee
sections.html:
The reported pump-yield median near Jefferson is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 2.0 and 7.0 gpm. The distribution is concentrated in the moderate range: 41% report 1 to 5 gpm, while 49% report 5 to 15 gpm. Only 4% report more than 15 gpm.

Low production still deserves attention. Six percent of reported wells yield under 1 gpm. That does not automatically make a property unusable, but it can require storage planning and careful household demand management. Have the driller explain the pumping test, recovery, pump setting, pressure tank, and storage approach. A well’s permit type and legal use also matter; 91% of these permits are for domestic or household use.

sections.heading: Water levels vary, and the decade record is uneven
sections.html:
Among Jefferson-area records that report a static water level, the median depth to water is 120 feet, with the middle half between 80 and 200 feet. That affects pump selection, electrical planning, and the length of drop pipe, but it is not the same as a well’s pumping yield.

The decade medians do not show a simple, steady decline. Reported depth to water was 95 feet in the 1970s, 70 feet in the 1980s, 85 feet in the 2000s, 170 feet in the 2010s, and 120 feet in the 2020s. The measurements come from different wells and years, so they should not be treated as a single monitoring well trend. A current static measurement and a pumping test are more useful for a specific purchase.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long-term drilling activity
sections.html:
Jefferson has a substantial permit record, with 2,418 wells in Colorado Division of Water Resources records and 1,609 marked as constructed. The newest permit year is 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 2000s, when 736 permits were issued, followed by 554 in the 1990s, 271 in the 1980s, and 229 in the 1970s.

The most active driller in these records is Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.), associated with 712 records. Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) appears on 163, and Whitewater Drilling Inc (Benkufski, John D.) on 140. Those records show local experience, but confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What drilling a Jefferson well can cost
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock, the local cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 345-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $22,400 to $34,500. That is drilling only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $28,400 to $46,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, and longer utility runs can change the final bid. Request a written allowance for mobilization, casing, grouting, testing, pump equipment, power, trenching, and any dry-hole terms. Compare bids on the same scope.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole exposure, and the building plan
sections.html:
Fractured-rock wells can vary in both yield and water quality. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that area. Those records do not prove a problem on a particular parcel, so test an existing well and review nearby land uses, mine history, and water-quality results before closing.

Low yield and a dry hole are separate risks from contamination. Confirm the permit, allowed household use, well location, septic reserve area, and building envelope together. A septic system, driveway, foundation, and well need workable separation and access. If construction is planned, have the site evaluated before buying rather than assuming the best drilling spot is also the best house site.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to plan a Jefferson purchase
sections.html:
Start with permits and construction reports for the parcel and nearby properties, especially around Como and the routes toward Fairplay, Alma, Hartsel, Bailey, and Blue River. Neighboring wells can show depth, casing, static level, yield, and the aquifer descriptions used in this mountain setting. They cannot guarantee the result, but they give a driller a better starting point than a broad regional average.

For an existing home, make the offer contingent on a well inspection, flow or pumping information, water-quality testing, and confirmation that the permitted use matches the property. For vacant land, budget around the local depth and finished-system ranges, then ask how added depth or difficult access is handled. Colorado DWR records and an experienced local driller should be part of the decision before you commit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Jefferson, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Jefferson is 345 feet. The middle half runs from 250 to 460 feet. About 54% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, while 9% exceed 600 feet. Fractured granite, gneiss, and other bedrock fractures make the actual depth on a parcel unpredictable.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Jefferson, Colorado?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in Jefferson’s fractured mountain bedrock. At the 345-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $22,400 to $34,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $28,400 to $46,500. Access, depth, and final equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Jefferson?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Jefferson is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 2.0 to 7.0 gpm. Forty-one percent report 1 to 5 gpm and 49% report 5 to 15 gpm. Six percent are under 1 gpm, so storage and household demand should be discussed before purchase.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Jefferson, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records show 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest after ownership or construction changes.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well near Jefferson?
faq.a: Many local permits are for domestic or household use, but the parcel’s permit and building plan must be checked together. Confirm the allowed use, well location, septic area, access, and water supply before buying. A driller should review nearby well records and the proposed site because fractured-bedrock yield can vary from one lot to the next.
